newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong crowds brave storm in rush for passports.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong crowds brave storm in rush for passports.

text.p: Big crowds braved Hong Kong's worst rainstorms in half century on Thursday to get new passports on the first working day under Chinese rule.
Hundreds jostled to collect or hand back application forms at the Immigration Tower in the bustling Wanchai district.
Others, having applied early, showed up to collect the new passports of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), as the former British colony is now known.
China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong on Monday night, ending 156 years of British colonial administration over this capitalist enclave of 6.4 million people.
Thursday was the first business day for the immigration office and for the rest of Hong Kong after a five-day extended handover holiday in celebration of the historic change of flag.
It was the first day of issue for the new passport, a deep blue document embossed with gold letters in Chinese and English and the five star seal of the People's Republic of China.
More than 700,000 application forms have been distributed to the public since applications started on June 10. The passports are ready for issue to those who applied first, three weeks ago.
Holders of the SAR document will be considered Chinese nationals as well as Hong Kong permanent residents.

So far about 40 countries, including Britain and the United States, have said they will grant visa-free or easy-visa access to SAR passports, a much better situation than existed for one of the passport's precursors, the Certificate of Identity (CI), which most countries viewed as a stateless person's document.
Almost every country required a visa in advance for CI holders, and it could be a long wait.
"I came this morning because my CI is going to expire soon and I am heading to Australia," said Lau Lai-ying as she stood in the scrum in the immigration office.
Some 5.5 million people are eligible for the new passport.
While most Hong Kong citizens regard the SAR passport as just a travel document, like Lau, some see it as a statement of nationhood and citizenship.
"Being a Hong Kong citizen, I must get myself an SAR passport. It indicates I'm a Chinese," said Cheung Hiu-kwan, a CI holder who came to Hong Kong eight years ago from China.
Members of Hong Kong's Pakistani minority are also attracted by the new passport.

Although he already holds a Pakistan and a British National Overseas (BNO) passport, Syedasad Ali said he was chasing the SAR passport. "If I have to cancel one passport, I'll cancel my BNO," he said.
Three million Hong Kong people are eligible to hold the BNO passport, which allows easy travel but provides no British residency rights.
